states.name: New York
states.framework: NYDFS BitLicense / Limited Purpose Trust Charter; proposed 23 NYCRR Part 202 (Authorized Payment Stablecoin Issuers)
states.regulator: New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS)
states.detail: Most coins commonly called “stablecoins” count as Virtual Currency under New York’s rules, which means issuing one requires a BitLicense or a New York-chartered trust company (the trust route also lets a company handle money transmission and fiduciary duties without extra licenses, which a BitLicense alone doesn’t allow). Before issuing, a coin also needs DFS sign-off through self-certification, a spot on DFS’s approved “Greenlist,” or individual approval. Coins already on the Greenlist include Gemini Dollar, Ripple USD, and WisdomTree Dollar. In July 2026, DFS proposed a new regulation, 23 NYCRR Part 202 (“Authorized Payment Stablecoin Issuers”), that reaffirms and aligns New York’s payment-stablecoin regime with the federal GENIUS Act. Part 202 takes effect on the GENIUS Act’s own effective date; it ties reserve, redemption, and attestation duties to the GENIUS Act (segregated per-brand reserves, monthly reserve-composition reports examined by a registered public accounting firm, and an annual attestation), gives issuers already approved by DFS 12 months to reach full compliance, and withdraws the department’s June 8, 2022 stablecoin guidance as of its effective date.
states.effective: In force now under the BitLicense / limited-purpose trust charter and DFS’s June 8, 2022 stablecoin guidance; proposed 23 NYCRR Part 202 takes effect on the GENIUS Act’s effective date (expected January 18, 2027) (replacing the 2022 guidance), with a 12-month compliance transition for existing issuers.
states.sourceText: NY DFS Virtual Currency Businesses; proposed 23 NYCRR Part 202, Authorized Payment Stablecoin Issuers (July 2026)
keyPoints: Today: hold a BitLicense or New York trust charter, and follow DFS’s 2022 stablecoin guidance (full 1:1 reserves, redemption at par, monthly CPA attestation)
Get DFS sign-off on the specific coin (self-certification, the approved Greenlist, or individual approval)
When Part 202 takes effect: back and segregate reserves per coin, file monthly reserve reports checked by an outside accounting firm, and get a yearly sign-off
Publish clear rules for how customers can cash out their coins
Already licensed? You have 12 months to meet the new Part 202 rules once they take effect
states.summary: New York already requires state approval to issue a stablecoin, and it already sets reserve, redemption, and attestation rules through existing DFS guidance. It has proposed updated rules (Part 202) that will replace that guidance and match the new federal GENIUS Act once the Act takes effect; firms already licensed then get a year to comply.

states.name: California
states.framework: Digital Financial Assets Law (DFAL)
states.regulator: California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI)
states.detail: California's Digital Financial Assets Law entered into force on July 1, 2026. Any exchange, custodian, stablecoin issuer, or Bitcoin ATM operator serving California residents must now hold a DFPI license or have filed a complete application, or face civil enforcement of up to $100,000 per day. The law bars licensees from exchanging a stablecoin unless its issuer is licensed, has applied for a license, or is a qualified bank or trust company backing the coin with eligible securities. DFPI expects an initial $100,000 net worth, subject to change, and began accepting applications through NMLS on March 9, 2026.
states.effective: In force since Jul. 1, 2026; DFPI license or complete application now required; enforcement active
states.sourceText: AB 39, Financial Code Div. 1.25
states.summary: California regulates digital-financial-asset (crypto) business activity under the Digital Financial Assets Law, licensed by the DFPI. Issuing a payment stablecoin is separately governed by the federal GENIUS Act.
keyPoints: Obtain a DFPI license under the Digital Financial Assets Law (DFAL) before engaging in digital-financial-asset business activity with California residents.
Meet the licensing law’s prudential requirements (surety bond or net worth, permissible investments or reserve holdings) and comply with AML, reporting, and consumer-disclosure obligations.

To issue a payment stablecoin, be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under the federal GENIUS Act (federally regulated, or a state-qualified issuer), separate from state money-transmission licensing.

states.name: Texas
states.framework: Money Services Modernization Act (Finance Code Ch. 152)
states.detail: Texas treats qualifying stablecoins as 'money,' which means issuing or transmitting them requires a money transmission license. To count, a stablecoin must be pegged to a currency like the dollar, fully backed by reserve assets, and redeemable for that currency on demand. Licensees must hold a minimum net worth that scales with their size, starting at $100,000. Texas also lets a licensee hold stablecoin itself as part of its required reserves, as long as it's the same stablecoin it owes to customers and is kept in proper custody.
states.effective: In force since Sept. 1, 2023
states.sourceText: Tex. Finance Code Ch. 152, enacted by S.B. 895 (2023)
states.summary: Texas licenses money transmission under its Money Services Modernization Act, which the Department of Banking applies to virtual currency. Issuing a payment stablecoin is separately governed by the federal GENIUS Act.
keyPoints: Obtain a Texas money-transmission license from the Department of Banking before transmitting money or virtual currency for Texas customers (Money Services Modernization Act, Finance Code ch. 152).
Meet the licensing law’s prudential requirements (surety bond or net worth, permissible investments or reserve holdings) and comply with AML, reporting, and consumer-disclosure obligations.

To issue a payment stablecoin, be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under the federal GENIUS Act (federally regulated, or a state-qualified issuer), separate from state money-transmission licensing.

states.name: Florida
states.framework: Money services business licensing (Fla. Stat. ch. 560) reaching virtual currency now; Florida Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 175) adds a stablecoin-issuer license from Oct. 1, 2026; SB 1568 pilot; HB 505 kiosks
states.detail: Florida regulates money services businesses under Chapter 560 of the Florida Statutes, administered by the Office of Financial Regulation (OFR). Virtual currency is treated as “monetary value,” so transmitting or exchanging it for others generally requires a Chapter 560 license, a view the OFR aligned with after Florida v. Espinoza. A 2022 amendment (CS/HB 273), effective January 1, 2023, added a statutory definition of “virtual currency” and eased the rules for direct two-party transactions, so a seller selling virtual currency straight to a buyer no longer needs a license, while third-party transmission remains licensable. On top of this, Florida enacted a package of stablecoin laws signed by Governor DeSantis on June 27, 2026. HB 175, the Florida Payment Stablecoin Act, requires a license from the OFR before issuing a payment stablecoin, with reserves backed one-to-one by cash or similarly safe assets and verified monthly by a CPA, aligning the state with the federal GENIUS Act; its licensing provisions take effect October 1, 2026. SB 1568 establishes a Stablecoin Pilot Program letting the Department of Financial Services accept approved payment stablecoins for certain government fees, effective on enactment. HB 505 requires virtual-currency kiosk operators to register with the OFR. Payment-stablecoin issuance also remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: Chapter 560 money-services licensing (reaching virtual currency; two-party VC sales exempt since Jan. 1, 2023) in force now; stablecoin package signed June 27, 2026, HB 175 issuer licensing effective Oct. 1, 2026; SB 1568 pilot and HB 505 kiosks effective on enactment
states.sourceText: Fla. Stat. ch. 560 (Money Services Businesses; virtual currency as monetary value; CS/HB 273 2022, eff. Jan. 1 2023); HB 175 Florida Payment Stablecoin Act (eff. Oct. 1, 2026); SB 1568 Stablecoin Pilot; HB 505 kiosks; FL Office of Financial Regulation
keyPoints: Today: hold a Florida money-services (Chapter 560) license to transmit or exchange virtual currency for others, through the Office of Financial Regulation
Direct two-party sales of virtual currency (seller straight to buyer) have been exempt from licensing since January 1, 2023 (CS/HB 273)
From October 1, 2026: to *issue* a payment stablecoin, get the new OFR license under HB 175, back reserves 1:1 with cash or safe assets, verified monthly by a CPA (aligned with the GENIUS Act)
Virtual-currency kiosk operators must register with the OFR (HB 505)
Florida is piloting acceptance of approved stablecoins for certain state fees (SB 1568)
states.summary: Florida already requires a state license to transmit or exchange virtual currency for others, though since 2023 a direct two-party sale (seller straight to buyer) is exempt. From October 1, 2026, a new law adds a dedicated license to *issue* a payment stablecoin, backed one-to-one by reserves checked monthly. Florida is also piloting acceptance of approved stablecoins for some state fees.

states.name: Wyoming
states.framework: Money-transmitter exemption for virtual currency (W.S. 40-22-104); Special Purpose Depository Institution charter (W.S. 13-12-101 et seq.); Wyoming Stable Token Act (W.S. 40-31-101 through 40-31-109; SF0127 / Enrolled Act No. 85, 2023), under which the state issues its own stablecoin
states.detail: Wyoming is the most distinctive state regime, and it works in three layers. First, private activity is exempt: the Wyoming Money Transmitters Act exempts virtual currency from licensing, so buying, selling, issuing, or taking custody of payment instruments in the form of virtual currency, or receiving virtual currency for transmission, does not require a money-transmitter license (W.S. 40-22-104). Wyoming defines these categories precisely: under W.S. 34-29-101, digital assets fall into three mutually exclusive classes, digital consumer assets, digital securities, and virtual currency, and a payment stablecoin (a medium of exchange that is not legal tender) generally sits in the “virtual currency” class the exemption covers. Second, a chartered-bank route exists: Wyoming created the Special Purpose Depository Institution (SPDI), a state bank charter designed to custody and handle digital assets (W.S. 13-12-101 et seq.), used by digital-asset banks such as Kraken Bank and Custodia. Third, and uniquely in the United States, the state issues its own stablecoin. Under the Wyoming Stable Token Act (W.S. 40-31-101 et seq.), the Wyoming Stable Token Commission issues the Frontier Stable Token (FRNT, launched as WYST in August 2025 and later rebranded), a virtual currency redeemable for one US dollar held in trust by the state (W.S. 40-31-104, 40-31-106). Under the Act’s reserve requirements as amended and the Commission’s rules, the token is backed only by cash, US Treasuries maturing within a year, or short-term Treasury repurchase agreements; a trust account holds 100% of the token’s notional value, plus a separate liquidity fund targeting a further 2% buffer, with surplus earnings directed quarterly to a state school foundation program. FRNT reached mainnet on August 18, 2025 and opened to public purchase on January 7, 2026 across eight blockchains. Private payment-stablecoin issuance also remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: Virtual currency exempt from money-transmitter licensing (W.S. 40-22-104); SPDI charter available (W.S. 13-12-101 et seq.); state-issued FRNT on mainnet since Aug. 18, 2025 and open to public purchase since Jan. 7, 2026
states.sourceText: W.S. 34-29-101 (digital-asset definitions: consumer asset / security / virtual currency); W.S. 40-22-104 (Money Transmitters Act virtual-currency exemption); W.S. 13-12-101 et seq. (SPDI charter); Wyoming Stable Token Act, W.S. 40-31-101 through 40-31-109 (SF0127 / Enrolled Act No. 85, 2023); Wyoming Stable Token Commission
keyPoints: No money-transmitter license is required to buy, sell, custody, or transmit virtual currency (including stablecoins) in Wyoming (W.S. 40-22-104)
Digital-asset banks can instead charter as a Special Purpose Depository Institution (SPDI) (W.S. 13-12-101 et seq.), the route used by Kraken Bank and Custodia
Wyoming itself issues a stablecoin, the Frontier Stable Token (FRNT), redeemable at $1.00 and fully reserved in cash and short US Treasuries
FRNT has been open to public purchase since January 7, 2026, live across eight blockchains
Private payment-stablecoin issuance remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act
states.summary: Wyoming is deliberately crypto-friendly and distinctive. It does not require a money-transmitter license to buy, sell, custody, or transmit virtual currency, including stablecoins. Instead it built bespoke structures: a special digital-asset bank charter (SPDI) and, uniquely, its own state-issued stablecoin, the Frontier Stable Token (FRNT).

states.name: Illinois
states.framework: Digital assets: Digital Assets and Consumer Protection Act (DACPA, 205 ILCS 731/) and Digital Asset Kiosks Act (DAKA, 205 ILCS 732/), plus the Digital Asset Tax Act (DATA, 35 ILCS 195/, enacted by SB 3019 / Public Act 104-0468). Money transmission: Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 3412), which repealed the Transmitters of Money Act effective Jan. 1, 2026.
states.regulator: Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation (IDFPR)
states.detail: Illinois has built a comprehensive digital-asset framework through four instruments, most of which phase in over 2026–2027. Money transmission was overhauled first: SB 3412 enacted the Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act and expressly repealed the Transmitters of Money Act effective January 1, 2026 (§ 900-30), moving Illinois to NMLS-based multistate licensing. Illinois did not adopt the model act’s optional virtual-currency provisions, so the money-transmission statute does not expressly reach virtual-currency or stablecoin transmission. Digital assets are instead addressed by two laws signed August 18, 2025. The Digital Assets and Consumer Protection Act (DACPA, 205 ILCS 731/, Public Act 104-0428) requires any person engaged in “digital asset business activity”, exchanging, transferring, or storing digital assets for Illinois residents, or digital-asset administration, to register with the Department of Financial and Professional Regulation (IDFPR). Its “digital asset” definition is drawn to capture stablecoins: assets not marketed for investment are generally excluded, except where the instrument is marketed to hold a nominal value “so stable as to render the nominal value effectively fixed.” DACPA’s prohibitions are not enforced until January 1, 2027, and registration is not required until July 1, 2027 (implementing rules may not take effect before January 1, 2026). The Digital Asset Kiosks Act (DAKA, 205 ILCS 732/, Public Act 104-0429) requires crypto-kiosk operators to register with IDFPR, caps daily kiosk transactions at $2,500 for new customers and $10,500 for existing customers, limits per-transaction fees to the greater of $5 or 18%, and mandates disclosures; existing operators must register by July 1, 2027. Finally, the Digital Asset Tax Act (DATA, 35 ILCS 195/), enacted as Article 3 of the FY2027 revenue bill (SB 3019, Public Act 104-0468), imposes, beginning January 1, 2027, a 0.2% tax on the privilege of receiving digital-asset business activity (exchanging, transferring, or storing digital assets) by an Illinois customer, collected by “digital asset brokers” (defined by reference to IRC § 6045(c)(1)(D)) and reaching out-of-state brokers whose gross receipts from Illinois customers reach $100,000 or more, tested quarterly. Returns and payment are due monthly, on or before the 20th, and the tax is administered by the Illinois Department of Revenue (the Act adopts DACPA’s definition of “digital asset,” so its stablecoin coverage carries into the tax). Illinois is therefore classified as phasing in: the dedicated regime is enacted but its core registration, kiosk, and tax obligations are not enforced until 2027.
states.effective: DACPA/DAKA core obligations enforced Jan. 1, 2027 and registration required by Jul. 1, 2027 (agency rules no earlier than Jan. 1, 2026); DATA (0.2% tax) effective Jan. 1, 2027 with broker registration before then; MTMA (SB 3412) effective Jan. 1, 2026 (Transmitters of Money Act repealed).
states.sourceText: “‘Digital asset’ … does not include … (4) A digital representation of value that is not marketed, used, promoted, offered, or sold for investment or speculation, except that this exclusion shall not apply to any digital representation of value that … (B) is marketed … in a manner that intends to establish a reasonable expectation or belief among the general public that the instrument will retain a nominal value that is so stable as to render the nominal value effectively fixed.” (DACPA, 205 ILCS 731/)
keyPoints: Today: money transmission is governed by the new Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 3412), which repealed the Transmitters of Money Act effective Jan. 1, 2026; Illinois did not adopt the model act’s optional virtual-currency provisions, so the money-transmission law does not expressly license virtual-currency or stablecoin transmission

From Jan. 1, 2027, DACPA (205 ILCS 731/): businesses that exchange, transfer, store, or administer digital assets for Illinois residents must register with IDFPR; the “digital asset” definition expressly captures stablecoins (instruments marketed to hold a nominal value “so stable as to render the nominal value effectively fixed”). Prohibitions enforced Jan. 1, 2027; registration required by Jul. 1, 2027

DAKA (205 ILCS 732/): crypto-kiosk operators must register with IDFPR; daily caps of $2,500 (new customers) and $10,500 (existing); per-transaction fees capped at the greater of $5 or 18%; existing operators register by Jul. 1, 2027

Digital Asset Tax Act (DATA, 35 ILCS 195/; SB 3019 / Public Act 104-0468, Art. 3): a 0.2% tax on the privilege of receiving digital-asset business activity (exchange, transfer, storage/custody) by a customer in Illinois, collected by “digital asset brokers,” reaching remote brokers with at least $100,000 in annual Illinois receipts (tested quarterly); returns and payment due monthly by the 20th; effective Jan. 1, 2027 (administered by the Illinois Department of Revenue)
states.summary: Illinois has enacted a comprehensive digital-asset framework, a consumer-protection registration law (DACPA), a crypto-kiosk law (DAKA), and the nation's first state digital-asset transaction tax (DATA), but the core obligations are not yet enforced and phase in over 2026–2027. Today, Illinois money-transmission law (the new Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act, which repealed the Transmitters of Money Act on Jan. 1, 2026) does not expressly reach virtual-currency transmission. From 2027, digital-asset businesses, stablecoin activity included, must register with IDFPR, and the transaction tax takes effect.

states.name: Colorado
states.framework: Model Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 25-1201)
states.detail: Colorado repealed its old Money Transmitters Act and replaced it with the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act, enabling multistate licensing participation. Unlike Texas, Colorado writes no virtual currency or stablecoin language into the statute at all: 'monetary value' is defined simply as 'a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money,' leaving it to interpretation whether a given stablecoin activity falls within that generic definition. Its net worth formula is identical to Texas's, since both states adopted the same model law: $100,000 or 3% of assets up to $100 million, then a declining percentage above that.
states.effective: Signed Apr. 18, 2025; effective Aug. 6, 2025
states.sourceText: Colorado General Assembly, HB 25-1201
states.summary: Colorado licenses money transmission, including virtual-currency transmission, under its Money Transmission Modernization Act. Issuing a payment stablecoin is separately governed by the federal GENIUS Act.
keyPoints: Obtain a Colorado money-transmitter license from the Division of Banking before transmitting virtual currency for Colorado residents (Money Transmission Modernization Act, HB 25-1201).
Meet the licensing law’s prudential requirements (surety bond or net worth, permissible investments or reserve holdings) and comply with AML, reporting, and consumer-disclosure obligations.

To issue a payment stablecoin, be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under the federal GENIUS Act (federally regulated, or a state-qualified issuer), separate from state money-transmission licensing.

states.name: Washington
states.framework: Washington Uniform Money Services Act (RCW ch. 19.230). The definition of “money transmission” includes virtual currency as “equivalent value” (RCW 19.230.010), so virtual-currency transmission requires a money-transmitter license.
states.regulator: Washington State Department of Financial Institutions
states.detail: Washington writes virtual currency directly into its money-transmission framework rather than creating a separate crypto license. Under the Uniform Money Services Act (RCW ch. 19.230), “money transmission” means receiving money or its equivalent value, where equivalent value includes virtual currency, to transmit or deliver to another location (RCW 19.230.010), and “virtual currency” is defined as a digital representation of value used as a medium of exchange, unit of account, or store of value lacking legal-tender status. Businesses transmitting virtual currency for Washington customers must be licensed by the Department of Financial Institutions, and virtual-currency licensees face additional requirements such as like-kind reserve holdings and security controls.
states.effective: In force
states.sourceText: Washington Uniform Money Services Act, RCW 19.230.010: “money transmission” includes virtual currency as equivalent value, so virtual-currency transmission requires a money-transmitter license.
states.summary: Washington writes virtual currency into its money-transmission definition, so virtual-currency transmission requires a money-transmitter license. Issuing a payment stablecoin is separately governed by the federal GENIUS Act.
keyPoints: Obtain a Washington money-transmitter license from the Department of Financial Institutions before transmitting virtual currency for Washington customers (Uniform Money Services Act, RCW 19.230.010, where “money transmission” includes virtual currency).
Virtual-currency licensees face additional requirements such as like-kind reserve holdings and security controls.

states.name: Arizona
states.framework: CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 1580, 2022)
states.regulator: Arizona Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions
states.detail: Arizona replaced its old money transmitter statute with the CSBS model act in 2022 (SB 1580, Chapter 236). Like Colorado, the new statute defines 'monetary value' as simply 'a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money,' with no explicit virtual currency or stablecoin definition. Whether a given stablecoin activity triggers licensing depends on how Arizona DIFI interprets that generic definition. Cryptocurrency kiosk operators face separate, explicit requirements under A.R.S. 6-1236, including daily transaction caps of $2,000 for new customers and $10,500 for existing ones, mandatory fraud warnings, and blockchain analytics requirements. Net worth follows the same formula as Colorado and Texas: $100,000 or 3% of total assets up to $100 million.
states.effective: Signed May 20, 2022
states.sourceText: A.R.S. Title 6, Chapter 12 (SB 1580, Ch. 236, 2022)
states.summary: In Arizona, virtual-currency money transmission requires a license under the Money Transmission Modernization Act. Issuing a payment stablecoin is separately governed by the federal GENIUS Act.
keyPoints: Obtain an Arizona money-transmitter license from the Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions (via NMLS) before transmitting virtual currency for Arizona residents (Money Transmission Modernization Act, SB 1580 (2022)).
Meet the licensing law’s prudential requirements (surety bond or net worth, permissible investments or reserve holdings) and comply with AML, reporting, and consumer-disclosure obligations.

states.name: Georgia
states.framework: Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 1272)
states.regulator: Georgia Department of Banking and Finance
states.detail: Georgia enacted the Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 1272) in 2026, a dedicated licensing regime for payment stablecoin issuers, but it is not yet in force. Under Section 4, and subject to appropriations by the General Assembly, it becomes effective on the earlier of January 18, 2027 or 120 days after the issuance of final federal GENIUS Act implementing regulations. The Act carves payment stablecoin issuance out of Georgia's existing money transmission laws and authorizes the Department of Banking and Finance to license issuers, on a framework the statute requires to be substantially similar to the GENIUS Act. Licensed issuers must back outstanding stablecoins one-to-one with liquid reserves held in trust for consumers and maintain redemption policies. Beginning July 18, 2028, it becomes unlawful to offer or sell a payment stablecoin in Georgia unless the issuer is a permitted, licensed, or federally qualified issuer. Separately, some virtual-currency money transmission already requires a license under O.C.G.A. Sec. 7-1-680 et seq.
states.effective: Enacted 2026; effective (subject to state appropriations) the earlier of Jan. 18, 2027 or 120 days after federal GENIUS Act final rules; issuer requirement from Jul. 18, 2028
states.sourceText: “Issuance of payment stablecoin shall not be considered to be money transmission as defined by Code Section 7-1-680.… Subject to appropriations by the General Assembly, this Act shall become effective upon the earlier of: (1) January 18, 2027; or (2) 120 days after the issuance of final implementing regulations for the GENIUS Act.” (HB 1272)
keyPoints: Today: transmitting or issuing a stablecoin requires a Georgia money transmitter license, “virtual currency” falls within the money-transmission definition (O.C.G.A. § 7-1-680), administered by the Department of Banking and Finance (recent enforcement: a Jan. 2026 cease-and-desist against a crypto-kiosk operator)

When the Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act takes effect (the earlier of Jan. 18, 2027 or 120 days after final GENIUS Act rules, subject to state appropriations): only a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue a payment stablecoin, licensed by the Department on a framework the statute requires to be “substantially similar to the GENIUS Act”

Once effective: issuing a payment stablecoin is no longer “money transmission” under § 7-1-680, a permitted issuer needs no separate money-transmission license to issue, sell, or redeem (but still needs one for other money-transmission activity)
From July 18, 2028: it is unlawful to offer or sell a payment stablecoin in Georgia unless it is issued by a licensed, permitted, or state qualified payment stablecoin issuer
states.summary: Georgia has enacted a dedicated stablecoin-issuer licensing law, the Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 1272), but it is not yet in force. Until it takes effect, issuing or transmitting a stablecoin in Georgia falls under the state's existing money-transmitter licensing. Once effective, stablecoin issuance moves to the new regime and is no longer treated as money transmission.

states.name: North Carolina
states.framework: Money Transmitters Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Ch. 53, Art. 16B)
states.regulator: North Carolina Office of the Commissioner of Banks
states.detail: North Carolina regulates stablecoin and virtual-currency activity through its Money Transmitters Act (Chapter 53, Article 16B), administered by the Office of the Commissioner of Banks (NCCOB). The statute expressly defines virtual currency and brings money transmission conducted in whole or in part in virtual currency, including maintaining control of virtual currency on behalf of others, within its licensing requirement. A person engaging in money transmission must obtain a license through NMLS; the license is perpetual but requires an annual NMLS renewal filing. North Carolina does not yet have a dedicated stablecoin-issuer statute. A separate bill, the Virtual Currency Kiosk Consumer Protection Act (HB 920), would place crypto-ATM operators under NCCOB supervision, with implementing rules due by December 1, 2026.
states.effective: Money Transmitters Act in force; virtual currency covered; kiosk bill (HB 920) pending, rules due Dec. 1, 2026
states.sourceText: N.C. Gen. Stat. Ch. 53, Art. 16B (Money Transmitters Act); NC Office of the Commissioner of Banks
states.summary: North Carolina licenses virtual-currency transmission under its Money Transmitters Act. Issuing a payment stablecoin is separately governed by the federal GENIUS Act.
keyPoints: Obtain a North Carolina money-transmitter license from the Office of the Commissioner of Banks before transmitting virtual currency for North Carolina residents (Money Transmitters Act, N.C. Gen. Stat. ch. 53, art. 16B).
Meet the licensing law’s prudential requirements (surety bond or net worth, permissible investments or reserve holdings) and comply with AML, reporting, and consumer-disclosure obligations.

To issue a payment stablecoin, be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under the federal GENIUS Act (federally regulated, or a state-qualified issuer), separate from state money-transmission licensing.

states.name: Connecticut
states.framework: Money Transmission Act (virtual currency revisions, PA 25-66 / HB 7082)
states.detail: Connecticut revised its money transmission law to regulate virtual currency, effective October 1, 2025, administered by the Department of Banking. A person engaged in virtual currency business in Connecticut, by receiving, transmitting, storing, or maintaining custody or control of virtual currency, must hold virtual currency of the same type and amount owed or obligated to each customer. Licensees may not lend, hypothecate, pledge, or otherwise use or encumber customer virtual currency without authorization, and the act extends risk-disclosure and receipt requirements to virtual currency transmitters and kiosk operators. Custody may be delegated only to parties qualified to hold it.
states.effective: In force since Oct. 1, 2025
states.sourceText: Conn. Public Act 25-66 (HB 7082); CT Dept. of Banking
states.summary: Connecticut’s Money Transmission Act covers virtual currency, as revised by PA 25-66 (HB 7082), so virtual-currency transmission requires a license. Issuing a payment stablecoin is separately governed by the federal GENIUS Act.
keyPoints: Obtain a Connecticut money-transmitter license from the Department of Banking before transmitting virtual currency for Connecticut residents (Money Transmission Act, virtual-currency revisions in PA 25-66 / HB 7082).
Meet the licensing law’s prudential requirements (surety bond or net worth, permissible investments or reserve holdings) and comply with AML, reporting, and consumer-disclosure obligations.

To issue a payment stablecoin, be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under the federal GENIUS Act (federally regulated, or a state-qualified issuer), separate from state money-transmission licensing.

states.name: Nevada
states.framework: CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act (NRS Ch. 671, enacted by A.B. 21, 2023); virtual currency covered by FID guidance
states.detail: Nevada enacted the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act through A.B. 21 (2023), modernizing its money transmission law at NRS Chapter 671, but it did not adopt the model's optional virtual-currency title (Article XIII). NRS Chapter 671 therefore does not expressly mention virtual or digital currency. Instead, the Financial Institutions Division (FID), through published guidance, applies the money-transmission licensing requirement to entities that transmit or hold digital currency, by kiosk, mobile, internet, or other means. Under that guidance, Bitcoin ATM operators must hold a money transmitter license and bond, and licensees holding virtual currency are expected to keep enough of each type to cover outstanding customer obligations. Entities acting purely as digital-asset custodians may instead be regulated as trust companies under NRS Chapter 669. Nevada thus regulates digital assets case by case under its MTMA-based money transmission law rather than a bespoke virtual-currency framework.
states.effective: MTMA enacted via A.B. 21 (2023) at NRS Ch. 671; digital currency covered by FID guidance, not the optional Article XIII virtual-currency title
states.sourceText: NRS Ch. 671, enacted by A.B. 21 (2023) adopting the CSBS Model MTMA without the optional virtual-currency title; digital currency covered by Nevada FID guidance
states.summary: Nevada adopted the Money Transmission Modernization Act, and the Financial Institutions Division’s guidance treats virtual-currency activity as covered. Issuing a payment stablecoin is separately governed by the federal GENIUS Act.
keyPoints: Obtain a Nevada money-transmitter license under NRS ch. 671 (Money Transmission Modernization Act, A.B. 21 (2023)) before engaging in covered virtual-currency activity; the Financial Institutions Division applies the Act to virtual currency by guidance.

To issue a payment stablecoin, be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under the federal GENIUS Act (federally regulated, or a state-qualified issuer), separate from state money-transmission licensing.

states.name: Maine

states.detail: Maine enacted the Maine Money Transmission Modernization Act through LD 2112 (signed April 22, 2024, effective August 9, 2024), codified in 32 M.R.S. ch. 80 and administered by the Bureau of Consumer Credit Protection. Maine is one of only three states (with Minnesota and North Dakota) to adopt the model act’s virtual-currency provisions: it defines virtual currency as a digital representation of value used as a medium of exchange, unit of account, or store of value that is not money, and requires a license for virtual-currency business activity, including exchanging, transferring, storing, or administering virtual currency (virtual-currency administration meaning issuing virtual currency with authority to redeem it for money, bank credit, or other virtual currency). The Bureau has begun issuing advisory rulings under the new statute.

states.framework: Sale of Checks and Transmission of Money Act (5 Del. C. Ch. 23); Money Transmission and Virtual Currency Modernization Act (SB 18, enacted 2026)

It takes effect the earlier of one year after enactment (around July 2027) or when the State Bank Commissioner promulgates final regulations.

states.detail: Virginia's Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 1942, enacted in 2025 as Acts of Assembly Chapter 214) takes effect July 1, 2026, replacing Chapter 19 of Title 6.2 with a new Chapter 19.1 administered by the State Corporation Commission's Bureau of Financial Institutions. Under Sec. 6.2-1922, 'money' does not include virtual currency, and because money transmission is defined in terms of money, payment instruments, and stored value, a business engaged solely in transmitting virtual currency, including a stablecoin, generally falls outside the licensing requirement. In practice the exclusion is narrower for stablecoins: activity that also moves fiat currency, such as redemption or on- and off-ramps, transmits 'money' and can still be captured. Federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.

states.name: South Carolina
states.framework: South Carolina Uniform Money Services Act (Title 35, Ch. 11; adopts the CSBS MTMA); S163 (2026) digital-asset exemptions
states.regulator: South Carolina Office of the Attorney General
states.detail: South Carolina regulates money transmission under the South Carolina Uniform Money Services Act (Title 35, Chapter 11), administered through the Attorney General's Money Services Division. (The chapter, originally the Anti-Money Laundering Act, was renamed by 2024 Act No. 218, effective July 2, 2024, which substantially adopted the CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act without its optional virtual-currency title.) The statute does not expressly address virtual currency, and the Money Services Division's interpretive position is that virtual currency does not, by itself, qualify as 'monetary value,' so virtual currency alone is not money transmission. South Carolina reinforced this by statute in 2026 with S163, which provides that a person exchanging a digital asset for another digital asset without the exchange of legal tender or bank deposits, or engaged in digital-asset mining, node operation, or blockchain software development, is not required to obtain a money transmitter license (S163 also bars state use of a central bank digital currency and protects self-custody). The exclusion remains narrower for stablecoins in practice: activity involving legal tender, such as redemption or on- and off-ramps, falls outside these exemptions and may require a license. Federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.

states.framework: Money Transmission Law (Ch. 312 of the Acts of 2024; MGL c. 169B)
states.detail: Massachusetts overhauled its money transmission regime with Chapter 312 of the Acts of 2024, codified as MGL c. 169B ('Regulation of Money Transmission') and administered by the Division of Banks. The Division began licensing and regulating money transmitters under c. 169B effective January 1, 2026 (NMLS applications opened around July 1, 2025). The Division has stated that most common transactional virtual currencies, expressly including stablecoins such as USDC, are a form of 'monetary value' under c. 169B, Sec. 1, so virtual-currency transmission requires a license. Non-convertible or closed-loop currencies (for example, in-game currency) are not 'monetary value.' The law is consumer-protection focused, covering money transmission for personal, family, or household purposes.

Operating a virtual-currency kiosk or transmitting virtual currency without a license violates Sec. 26-1002 and can carry civil and criminal penalties.

states.detail: Tennessee regulates money transmission under the Tennessee Money Transmitter Act (Tenn. Code Ann. title 45, ch. 7). In its Virtual Currency Guidance, the Department of Financial Institutions takes the position that cryptocurrency is not “money” under the Act, so holding or transmitting pure virtual currency is not money transmission and the money-transmitter license does not cover it. Absent a sovereign currency in the transaction, no money transmission occurs. However, a company that exchanges, administers, or maintains virtual currency for sovereign currency may be subject to state licensing (and to federal regulation), because that activity involves the transmission of sovereign currency.

states.detail: Louisiana runs one of the most developed state regimes: the Virtual Currency Businesses Act (VCBA), La. Rev. Stat. §§ 6:1381 to 6:1394, adopted in 2020, made Louisiana the second state after New York to create a dedicated, standalone licensing scheme for virtual-currency business activity. states.name: Oklahoma
states.framework: Oklahoma Financial Transaction Reporting Act (6 O.S. §§ 1511–1515) through Oct. 31, 2026; Oklahoma Money Transmission Modernization Act (6 O.S. § 1551) from Nov. 1, 2026, defining “money” to include qualifying stablecoins; digital-asset kiosks under § 1520.1
states.detail: Oklahoma licenses money transmission, and virtual-currency exchanges operating in the state hold Oklahoma money-transmitter licenses. Through October 31, 2026, licensing runs under the Oklahoma Financial Transaction Reporting Act (6 O.S. §§ 1511–1515), whose definition of “money transmitter” is fiat-centric: it reaches a person who accepts and transmits “currency or funds denominated in currency” (legal tender), or the value of that currency (6 O.S. § 1512). The Act does not expressly name virtual currency, so crypto firms are captured mainly through their fiat on- and off-ramp activity. The one express digital-asset provision is 6 O.S. § 1520.1 (SB 1083, 2025), regulating digital-asset kiosks (crypto ATMs): operators must be licensed as money transmitters, cap new-customer activity at $2,000 per day, limit aggregate fees to 15% per transaction, give prominent fraud warnings, provide receipts, refund fraudulently-induced customers, run blockchain-analytics screening, and employ a full-time compliance officer, with unlicensed operation a misdemeanor and kiosks subject to seizure by the Attorney General. Effective November 1, 2026, the Oklahoma Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 3521) repeals §§ 1511–1515 and recodifies money transmission at 6 O.S. § 1551, and, unlike the old act, expressly defines “money” to include a stablecoin that is (a) pegged to a sovereign currency, (b) fully backed by assets held in reserve, and (c) redeemable for sovereign currency from the issuer; the kiosk provisions (§§ 1520, 1520.1) are retained with their cross-reference updated. Non-stablecoin virtual currency (e.g., Bitcoin) is not “money” under either act. Payment-stablecoin issuance also remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.

states.name: Utah
states.framework: Utah Money Transmitter Act (Utah Code § 7-25-102): the definition of “money transmission” excludes a blockchain token, so standalone virtual-currency transmission is not licensed. HB 72 (2026) carves virtual-currency kiosks back into licensing.
states.detail: Utah does not require a money-transmitter license for standalone virtual-currency transmission. The Money Transmitter Act’s definition of “money transmission” expressly excludes a “blockchain token” (Utah Code § 7-25-102), a 2020 change confirming that ordinary cryptocurrency transactions are not money transmission, so crypto firms are generally exempt. HB 72 (2026) creates an exception: operating a virtual-currency kiosk in Utah requires a license under the Money Transmitter Act and constitutes money transmission regardless of whether the transactions involve blockchain tokens. The Department of Financial Institutions administers the Act through the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System (NMLS).

states.name: New Mexico
states.framework: New Mexico Uniform Money Services Act (NMSA 1978 § 58-32-102 (definitions); § 58-32-201 (license required)). Virtual currency is reached by regulator interpretation of “monetary value,” not by an express virtual-currency statute.
states.regulator: New Mexico Financial Institutions Division (Regulation and Licensing Department)
states.detail: New Mexico requires a money-transmitter license to deal in virtual currency, reaching that result by regulator interpretation rather than express statute. The Uniform Money Services Act defines “money transmission” as receiving money or monetary value for transmission, and “monetary value” as “a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money” (NMSA 1978 § 58-32-102). The Regulation and Licensing Department’s Financial Institutions Division (FID) has stated that any business exchanging virtual currency for money, monetary value, or stored value for New Mexico residents must be licensed as a money transmitter under § 58-32-201.

states.name: West Virginia
states.framework: West Virginia Money Transmission Modernization Act (W. Va. Code § 32A-2-1 et seq., as amended by HB 5353 (2026)). “Money transmission” expressly reaches virtual currency (control of virtual currency, virtual-currency kiosks, digital wallets, and exchange).

states.detail: West Virginia’s money transmission statute, W. Va. Code § 32A-2 (the Money Transmission Modernization Act), expressly reaches virtual currency. Section 32A-2-1 defines “control of virtual currency,” “digital wallet,” and “exchange” (which includes virtual currency), and the definition of “money transmission” includes “engaging in the business of owning or operating a virtual currency kiosk.” HB 5353 (2026) amended § 32A-2-1 and related sections to modernize licensing and bring virtual-currency activity, including kiosks, within money-transmission licensure. (The tracker’s prior citation to HB 2585 (2019) was incorrect; HB 2585 was a 2017 money-laundering measure.) The Division of Financial Institutions administers the Act.

states.name: Vermont
states.framework: Vermont money transmission law (8 V.S.A. ch. 79), amended by Act 110 (2023 Adj. Sess., effective July 1, 2024) to include virtual-currency business activity; virtual-currency kiosk operators are governed by 8 V.S.A. § 2577.
states.detail: Vermont overhauled its money-transmission law through Act 110 (2023 Adj. Sess.), effective July 1, 2024, adopting the Money Transmission Modernization Act and bringing virtual-currency business activity within licensing: persons exchanging, storing, or transmitting virtual currency, or receiving virtual currency or control of it for transmission, as a business must be licensed by the Department of Financial Regulation. The Department of Financial Regulation administers the law.

states.name: Wisconsin
states.framework: Wisconsin Money Transmission Modernization Act (Wis. Stat. ch. 217), enacted by 2023 Wisconsin Act 267 (effective Jan. 1, 2025), replacing the former Seller of Checks law. General virtual-currency transmission is not licensed; virtual-currency kiosks are regulated under Wis. Stat. § 217.12.
states.detail: Wisconsin does not license general virtual-currency or stablecoin transmission. 2023 Wisconsin Act 267 (signed April 4, 2024, effective January 1, 2025) repealed the former Seller of Checks law (the prior Wis. Stat. ch. 217) and replaced it with the Money Transmission Modernization Act, now codified at Wis. Stat. ch. 217. Wisconsin adopted the model act without its optional virtual-currency provisions, so transmitting virtual currency by itself generally does not require a Wisconsin money-transmitter license, though a business handling both virtual and fiat currency may need one for the fiat leg. The Act does expressly regulate virtual-currency kiosks under Wis. Stat. § 217.12, imposing antifraud, disclosure, and customer-identification requirements on kiosk operators. The Department of Financial Institutions administers the Act.
